# Editorial overview

These problems share one discipline: define the cumulative family before
inverting it. A formula containing `mu`, `phi`, or a divisor loop is not yet a
solution; the proof must say which objects each term counts.

| Problem | Cumulative family | Recovery step |
|---|---|---|
| A | pairs whose two values are divisible by `d` | expand `gcd^k` over its divisors |
| B | totients weighted by the number of multiples | isolate the summatory function and group quotients |
| C | pairs whose lcm divides `m` | subtract exact proper-divisor counts |
| D | integers divisible by each square `d^2` | Mobius inclusion-exclusion, then binary search |

# A. GCD Pair Energy

## Restatement and constraints

We need the sum of `gcd(ai,aj)^k` over all `i<j`. Enumerating pairs is
quadratic; factorizing each pair does not repair that. The value bound
`M <= 200000` suggests sieve loops over all multiples.

## Finding the transform

Define `J[d]` by the divisor identity

```text
x^k = sum(J[d] for d dividing x).
```

We can compute it without memorizing a closed form. Start with `J[x]=x^k` and
subtract `J[d]` from every proper multiple of `d`, processing `d` increasingly.
When `J[x]` is reached, every proper-divisor contribution has been removed.

For one pair with gcd `g`, its energy becomes

```text
g^k = sum(J[d] for d dividing g).
```

The condition `d | gcd(ai,aj)` is exactly “`d` divides both values.” If
`cnt[d]` input values are multiples of `d`, precisely `C(cnt[d],2)` pairs
receive the contribution `J[d]`.

## Worked trace

For `2,4,6` and `k=2`, inversion of `x^2` begins

```text
J[1]=1
J[2]=4-J[1]=3
J[3]=9-J[1]=8
J[4]=16-J[1]-J[2]=12
```

All three values are divisible by `2`, so `J[1]*C(3,2) + J[2]*C(3,2)`
already gives `3+9=12`. Larger divisors contain fewer than two values.

## Algorithm

1. Build value frequencies.
2. For every `d`, sum frequencies at `d,2d,3d,...` into `cnt[d]`.
3. Set `J[d]=d^k`; invert its divisor sums in increasing order.
4. Add `J[d]*cnt[d]*(cnt[d]-1)/2` for every `d`.

## Correctness proof

**Lemma 1.** After the inversion loop, `x^k` equals the sum of `J[d]` over
all divisors `d` of `x`.

**Proof.** When processing `x`, its initial value is `x^k`. Each already
finalized proper divisor `d` subtracts `J[d]` exactly once. Therefore the
remaining value is the unique amount required to make the divisor sum equal
`x^k`. Induction over increasing `x` proves the identity. QED.

**Lemma 2.** `C(cnt[d],2)` is the number of pairs whose gcd is divisible by
`d`.

**Proof.** Their gcd is divisible by `d` exactly when both values are divisible
by `d`; choosing two of the `cnt[d]` qualifying indices counts each pair once.
QED.

**Theorem.** The algorithm prints the required energy sum.

**Proof.** By Lemma 1, each pair of gcd `g` contributes `J[d]` once for every
`d|g`. By Lemma 2, the outer sum counts exactly all pairs receiving each such
contribution. Thus every pair contributes exactly `g^k`. QED.

## Complexity and tests

Both sieve loops cost `O(M log M)` and memory is `O(M)`. Modular powers add
`O(M log k)`. Test `k=0`, all ones, all equal values, and values with several
shared divisors.

# B. Summatory Totient

## Why the ordinary sieve is insufficient

A sieve to `n` is excellent when `n` is a few million. It cannot allocate an
array of length `10^9`. We need a recurrence whose distinct arguments are the
few values of `floor(n/i)`.

## Derivation

Start from `sum_{d|m} phi(d)=m` and sum over `m=1..n`:

```text
sum_{d=1..n} phi(d) * floor(n/d) = n(n+1)/2.
```

There is another way to expose the desired prefix. Count the same left side by
the quotient `q=floor(n/d)`. Equivalently, isolate the copy of every `phi(d)`
whose multiplier includes at least one and recursively remove the extra
copies. This yields

```text
Phi(n) = n(n+1)/2 - sum_{l=2..n} Phi(floor(n/l)).
```

Equal quotients are repeated. If `q=floor(n/l)`, it remains equal through
`r=floor(n/q)`, so the whole block subtracts
`(r-l+1)*Phi(q)`.

For `n=10`, the blocks starting at two are

```text
[2,2] -> 5, [3,3] -> 3, [4,5] -> 2, [6,10] -> 1.
```

## Algorithm

Precompute `Phi` through `10^6`. For a larger argument, initialize its answer
to the triangular number, traverse quotient blocks starting at `2`, recursively
subtract each block contribution, and memoize the result.

## Correctness proof

**Lemma 1.** The ungrouped recurrence for `Phi(n)` is valid.

**Proof.** In the divisor identity summed through `n`, `phi(d)` occurs once for
each multiple of `d`, hence `floor(n/d)` times. Removing the first occurrence
of every `phi(d)` leaves the extra occurrences; regrouping them by the chosen
multiple produces `sum_{l=2..n} Phi(floor(n/l))`. The remaining first copies
sum to `Phi(n)`. QED.

**Lemma 2.** The grouped loop equals the ungrouped sum.

**Proof.** The formula for `r` gives the maximal consecutive interval on which
`floor(n/i)=q`. Multiplying `Phi(q)` by its interval length accounts for every
index in that interval once. The intervals are disjoint and cover `2..n`.
QED.

**Theorem.** Every returned value is `Phi(n)` modulo the modulus.

**Proof.** Small values are exact sieve prefixes. For a larger value, all
recursive arguments are smaller. Strong induction with Lemmas 1 and 2 proves
the computed recurrence exact; memoization changes only repeated work. QED.

## Complexity and tests

The precomputation uses `O(B log log B)` time and `O(B)` memory for
`B=10^6`. Harmonic blocking and memoization give the standard sublinear
summatory-function behavior; for this bound it is comfortably below a linear
sieve to `n`. Test around `B`, repeated queries, and compare with a direct
totient sieve for random `n <= 500`.

# C. LCM Pair Spectrum

## Observation

For a fixed `m`, let `inside[m]` be the number of input values dividing `m`.
Any pair chosen among them has lcm dividing `m`, and every pair whose lcm
divides `m` has both values dividing `m`. Therefore

```text
C(inside[m],2) = sum(exact[d] for d dividing m).
```

This equivalence is the entire reduction. It changes a two-value operation
(`lcm`) into two one-dimensional divisor transforms.

## Trace

For `1,2,3,6`, `inside[6]=4`, so six pairs have lcm dividing six. We already
recover one pair at lcm two and one at lcm three; none has lcm one. Subtracting
these proper-divisor spectra leaves four pairs at lcm six.

## Algorithm

1. Sieve each frequency into all of its multiples to obtain `inside`.
2. Initialize `exact[m]=C(inside[m],2)`.
3. In increasing order, subtract `exact[d]` from every proper multiple of `d`.

## Correctness proof

**Lemma 1.** Before inversion, `exact[m]` (temporarily) counts pairs whose lcm
divides `m`.

**Proof.** As shown above, this family is exactly the pairs drawn from values
that divide `m`, of which there are `C(inside[m],2)`. QED.

**Lemma 2.** After processing index `m`, `exact[m]` counts pairs whose lcm is
exactly `m`.

**Proof.** By increasing induction, every exact count for a proper divisor is
already known and subtracted once. Lemma 1 says the cumulative count contains
only exact lcms dividing `m`; the remainder is exactly lcm `m`. QED.

The theorem follows from Lemma 2 for every output position.

## Complexity and tests

Time is `O(M log M+n)` and memory is `O(M)`. Test repeated equal values,
many ones, prime values, and an `M` larger than every input value.

# D. Square-Free Rank

## From a slow recognizer to a prefix counter

Checking every integer and factorizing it would require work proportional to
the answer. Instead count how many valid integers are at most `X`.

An integer is divisible by no prime square. Inclusion-exclusion over prime
squares can be packaged by the Mobius function:

```text
count(X) = sum mu(d) * floor(X/(d*d)), for d*d <= X.
```

If `d` is square-free with `t` prime factors, `mu(d)=(-1)^t`, exactly the
inclusion-exclusion sign for being divisible by those `t` prime squares. If
`d` itself contains a square, `mu(d)=0`, so a repeated condition contributes
nothing.

## Trace

For `X=10`:

```text
d=1: +10
d=2: -floor(10/4) = -2
d=3: -floor(10/9) = -1
total: 7
```

Indeed `1,2,3,5,6,7,10` are the seven square-free values.

## Algorithm

Sieve `mu` up to the square root of the largest binary-search upper bound.
For every rank, binary-search the smallest `X` for which `count(X)>=k`.
`3k` is a safe course bound; the density of square-free integers is bounded
away from zero, and the implementation can also double the bound if desired.

## Correctness proof

**Lemma 1.** `count(X)` equals the number of square-free integers at most `X`.

**Proof.** Fix an integer `x`. Its total coefficient in the sum is
`sum_{d*d|x} mu(d)`. This is one when no prime square divides `x`, and zero
otherwise by inclusion-exclusion. Summing those indicators over `x<=X` gives
the formula. QED.

**Lemma 2.** The binary search returns the k-th square-free integer.

**Proof.** `count(X)` is monotone. At the returned smallest `X`, at least `k`
valid values are no larger than `X`, while fewer than `k` are no larger than
`X-1`. Therefore `X` itself is precisely the k-th. QED.

## Complexity and tests

For one query, each count costs `O(sqrt(X))` and binary search uses `O(log X)`
counts. The Mobius sieve uses `O(sqrt(max X))` memory. Test ranks surrounding
perfect squares and compare the first several hundred answers with trial
division.

# Stress-testing strategy

The supplied randomized tests deliberately use tiny domains and independent
brute definitions: explicit pairs for A and C, direct gcd counts for phi in B,
and trial square divisibility in D. This is stronger than comparing two
implementations of the same optimized formula.

# What to carry forward

When a hard arithmetic problem asks for exact gcd/lcm classes, first count an
easier cumulative divisibility family. When `floor(n/i)` appears, enumerate its
constant intervals. When the target is the k-th valid integer, search on a
proven prefix-count oracle.
